subject: Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations

messages.author: f7c335e987e6a186
messages.subject: Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations
parts:
Hi folks,

This is more a theoretical rather than dartR specific technical question, but what would be an appropriate method to determine whether genetic diversity (measured either by observed heterozygosity or allelic richness or both) for subpopulations of a given study species are significantly different from each other, and to determine say 95% confidence intervals?

This is for DArT SNP data. Say there are 10 subpopulations each sampled from distinct locations with n ranging from 8 to 30 and around 3,000 SNPs remaining after filtering for <5% missing data (or fewer SNPs for calculations of allelic richness based on no missing data).

Thanks,
Peter

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations
parts:
Hi Peter,

There is a dartR function that does exactly what you want. Can you try in the developing version of dartR:

> gl.install.vanilla.dartR(flavour = "dev")

> gl.test.heterozygosity(platypus.gl)

Cheers,
Luis

messages.author: b3d929c6746ca81a
messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations
parts:
Hi Peter
Just brief. I would use a power analysis using allele frequencies of the individuals from a pair of population combined and sample using your sample sizes and calculate difference in heterozygosity. 
Rerun a 1000 times or so and then  you get a “null distribution and you can check if your value is outside the say 95% conf interval. 

The function gl.sim.ind can be used for this. 


Re do for each of the pairs and use a bonferroni correction to be sure. 
Hope that makes sense,
Cheers Bernd

---------

messages.author: 86913d3f72f6633b
messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations
parts:
Hi Peter,
while Bernd approach is perfectly valid, the other option you could consider is to use Jackknife resampling (over individuals, within populations) to compute the metric's standard error (this is what Fstat would do) and from there its confidence interval. If CIs are not overlapping between a pair of pops, then they are significantly different. There is a new function on the dev branch that conducts Jackknife resampling in dartR (utils.jackknife). Note, that this approach probably lacks stat power for those populations where the sample size is small (something that Bernd's approach probably deals with more elegance).

Cheers,
carlo

messages.author: b3d929c6746ca81a
messages.subject: RE: [dartR] Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations
parts:
Hi Carlo,

 

Your approach made me thinking what the difference between our suggestions are.

 

My “current” understanding is

 

Your approach checks if sample sizes are affecting the results

 

My suggestion is tailored towards the idea: is there a difference between the pair assuming they have originated from a common population (+including the sample size issue when samples are drawn in accordance with the actual sample size).

 

@Peter: it depends now what your actual question is:

 

Carlos version: What is the power to detect a difference given the sample size.

 

My version: the two populations are actually one (=NULL). Is my result extreme enough to reject the NULL?

 

 

Hope that makes sense,

 

Bernd

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Significance of differences in heterozygosity between subpopulations
parts:
Thank you Bernd, Luis and Carlo for your suggestions.

To perhaps clarify, I'm wanting to rank, or at least group the 10 subpopulations from most genetically diverse to least where that's justified, but with the null hypothesis that they are all actually pretty much equally diverse with observed differences simply due to random sampling error. So I think what I'm after is closer to what Bernd has suggested. It's likely only some of the pairwise comparisons will be significant.

Cheers,
Peter
